# The Future of Work: A Design Proposal for Global Endorsement and Local Adaptation

**Prepared for:** Executive Committee, with parallel circulation to Regional Leadership, Group Finance, Real Estate, IT, Legal & Tax, Group Security, and — where statutory bodies exist — to works councils and employee representatives *before* any external communication.

**Status:** Recommended design. All financial figures are illustrative placeholders pending validation by Group Finance and Real Estate; all statutory timelines require confirmation by local Legal counsel. Sections marked **[Requires consultation]** are not to be presented as decided in the affected jurisdictions.

---

## 1. Executive Summary

**The recommendation in three lines.** Stop asking how many days people should be in the office. Instead, (a) match work type to genuine co-location need, (b) push design decisions to the value-stream level within a deliberately thin global core, and (c) extend a comparable *flexibility investment per head* to desk-based and deskless populations alike — in different currencies, but at similar value.

**What it costs and what it returns (illustrative, to be validated).** For a company of ~60,000 people across ~40 countries, of whom roughly 40% are desk-based:

| Item | 3-year illustrative figure |
|---|---|
| Current annual property cost (rent, service charge, energy, FM) | €430m |
| Leases expiring or with break options within 36 months | ~34% of portfolio by cost |
| Net property saving from recommended portfolio scenario (regional hub-and-spoke) | €95–130m p.a. by year 3 |
| Reinvestment: fit-out quality, hub network, gathering travel, tooling, deskless amenity and scheduling systems | €55–70m p.a. |
| Home-working allowances and equipment (desk-based) | €18–24m p.a. |
| Manager and leader enablement (build + delivery) | €9m one-off, €3m p.a. |
| **Net structural saving retained** | **€25–45m p.a.** |

**Where the upside actually sits** — and this is the part that turns the programme from a cost exercise into a strategy one:

- **Hiring radius.** Access to 6–8 additional metropolitan labour markets per region without new legal entities, using the tiered mobility model in §10.
- **Offer acceptance and retention.** Flexibility is now a top-three factor in candidate decisions in most of our markets; a defensible, differentiated position is worth more than the property saving.
- **Follow-the-sun and resilience.** Distributed capability materially improves business continuity and reduces single-site concentration risk.
- **Carbon.** Commuting and portfolio reduction contribute measurably to stated Scope 1–3 targets; the offsetting increase in gathering travel must be counted honestly (see §5.4).

**What we ask of the Executive Committee.** Not approval of a rulebook — endorsement of seven principles, a governance body, a property scenario aligned to the lease calendar, and a set of stated positions on pay, mobility and stability. And, in Phase 0, a documented commitment from each Executive Committee member regarding their own working pattern. Nothing else in this document will survive if that step is skipped.

**A note on how we propose to proceed.** This design has been shaped by early listening across regions and, deliberately, has not been finalised. Several elements require formal consultation before they can be presented as decided. We would rather move a quarter more slowly and arrive with agreement intact than announce a scheme that quietly loses the confidence of colleagues and their representatives.

---

## 2. Seven Principles

**Principle 1 — Purpose over presence.**
Time and location are inputs; contribution is the output. Where they can be decoupled, decouple them. Where they genuinely cannot — production lines, laboratories, client sites, regulated environments, secure facilities — the constraint is stated with its reason, and Principle 7 applies instead.

**Principle 2 — A thin centre, thick edges.**
The centre owns only what must be common: legal and tax compliance, security, equity measurement, the tooling backbone, and a short list of non-negotiables. Rhythms, meeting norms, office use and rituals belong closer to the work. A short list of global rules is easier to respect than a long one.

**Principle 3 — The value stream is the unit of design.**
Friction lives in the interfaces between people, not in individuals working alone. Working agreements are therefore authored at the level of interdependency — the value stream, product line or service chain — not the org chart box (§6).

**Principle 4 — Flexibility must be equitably distributed, and measured.**
Flexibility that flows to the senior, the confident, the geographically central or the well-housed is a privilege, not a benefit. We assume proximity bias and time-zone burden exist until measurement shows otherwise.

**Principle 5 — Local adaptation is a feature, not a compliance failure.**
Divergence between Singapore, Munich and Monterrey is evidence the framework is working. What must be consistent is the fairness of outcomes, not the shape of arrangements.

**Principle 6 — Learn openly, but do not destabilise lives.**
Arrangements carry review dates; individuals carry stability guarantees (§12.3). Reversibility at the system level is paired with notice periods at the personal level, because colleagues make housing, schooling and eldercare decisions on the strength of what we tell them.

**Principle 7 — Flexibility for all, in different currencies.**
Every colleague receives a flexibility investment; its form differs by role. For deskless colleagues that means predictability, control over time, and quality of the on-site day. The commitment is that **flexibility investment per head is broadly comparable across populations**, and reported as such. This principle exists to prevent the outcome we consider the single largest risk in the programme: a two-tier culture in which one population receives autonomy and the other receives an explanation.

---

## 3. Two Populations, One Commitment

Roughly 60% of our colleagues cannot choose their location. A framework that speaks only to the other 40% would damage cohesion in exactly the places where cohesion is hardest won — plants, depots, contact centres, retail and field service.

**The deskless flexibility package (recommended standard):**

| Element | Commitment |
|---|---|
| Schedule notice | Rosters published ≥ 3 weeks ahead; no unilateral change inside 7 days without premium |
| Shift swapping | Self-service, peer-to-peer, manager-approved by exception only |
| Compressed and split patterns | Available where safety and coverage permit; requests answered within 10 working days with a reason |
| Banked time / time-account | Accrual and withdrawal within statutory limits, portable across the year |
| Part-remote elements of deskless roles | Training, admin, planning, debriefs shifted off-site where feasible — typically 5–15% of hours |
| On-site quality | Quiet rooms, decent break space, lockers, connectivity, parking/transport support, heating and cooling |
| Voice | Frontline representation on the Work Design Council; site-level design volunteers |
| Career access | Remote-accessible training and internal mobility; no advancement path that requires relocation without support |

**Reporting.** The equity scorecard (§11) reports flexibility investment per head, request-approval rates, and schedule-stability performance separately for deskless and desk-based populations. Where a gap opens, it is a Council agenda item, not a footnote.

**[Requires consultation]** In unionised sites, scheduling and time-account provisions are subject to collective bargaining. We recommend approaching representatives with the *principle* and a genuine blank on the mechanism, rather than a finished scheme.

---

## 4. Architecture and Governance

### 4.1 The four layers

| Layer | Owns | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Global core** (minimal) | Non-negotiables | Employment/tax compliance, security standards, pay and promotion equity, tooling backbone, measurement, ethical floor (accessibility, rest and disconnection with the on-call carve-out in §8.4) |
| **Region / country** | Legal and cultural translation | Statutory consultation, labour law, office portfolio, allowances calibrated to local cost and housing, holiday and time-zone conventions |
| **Value stream / team** | The real design work | Working agreement: overlap band, meeting-free blocks, async defaults, in-person cadence and purpose, decision rights, response norms |
| **Individual** | Personal fit | Where and when within the agreement, workspace, negotiated exceptions (caregiving, health, accessibility, visa) |

An outer layer may constrain an inner one, but must record why. Operationally: the constraint is logged in the Work Design Register with a named owner, a category (legal / security / customer coverage / cost / safety), and a review date. Unrecorded constraints lapse at the next quarterly review. Appeals go to the Council, which answers within 15 working days.

### 4.2 Governance

**Work Design Council.** Chaired by the Chief People Officer; sponsored by the COO as named Executive owner. Members: HR, Real Estate & Workplace, IT, Legal & Tax, Group Security, Finance, plus **six rotating seats** — three regional representatives and three non-managerial colleagues (at least one deskless). Quarterly, with a monthly working group.

**Decision rights (summary RACI):**

| Decision | Accountable | Consulted |
|---|---|---|
| Global non-negotiables; ethical floor | Executive Committee | Council; employee representatives |
| Portfolio scenario, capital, lease action | Real Estate, with CFO | Region; Council |
| Country policy translation; allowances | Regional HR lead | Legal; works council; Finance |
| Working agreements; in-person cadence | Value-stream leader | Interdependent teams; team members |
| Individual arrangements | Line manager | HR partner where an exception applies |
| Cross-border remote requests | Global Mobility | Tax, Legal, Security |
| Exceptions and appeals | Work Design Council | Requesting party |

**Service levels.** Individual arrangement requests: answered in 10 working days. Cross-border requests: 20. Escalated inter-team conflicts: resolved by the shared leader within 5 working days, or referred upward automatically. Silence is not an answer; unanswered requests default to "granted provisionally, pending review."

---

## 5. Property Portfolio and the Financial Case

### 5.1 The lease calendar is the forcing function

Property decisions run on a multi-year clock that will not wait for pilot results. We therefore recommend sequencing decisions by expiry, not by programme phase:

| Horizon | Portfolio share (illustrative) | Recommended posture |
|---|---|---|
| 0–12 months | 11% by cost | Decide now on scenario logic; prefer short extensions to preserve optionality |
| 12–36 months | 23% | Decide by end of Design phase; pilots inform fit-out, not footprint |
| 36 months+ | 66% | Decide after pilots; use the interval to improve occupancy data |

### 5.2 Scenarios

| Scenario | Footprint change | Annual cost effect | Capacity | Principal risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Hold** | 0% | – | 100% | Pays for empty space; signals no change |
| **B. Consolidate to fewer, larger sites** | –25% | –€105m | 70% at 1:1.4 sharing | Longer commutes; concentration risk; poorest fit with local housing realities |
| **C. Regional hub-and-spoke** *(recommended)* | –22% desk area, +14 small hubs | –€95m gross, –€60m net of hub cost and fit-out | 85% at 1:1.6 | Operational complexity; requires disciplined booking data |
| **D. Radical distributed** | –45% | –€180m | 45% | High attrition risk in offices that function as social and mentorship centres; hard to reverse |

We recommend **C**, on grounds of reversibility and reduced disruption to established site communities. D produces the larger number and, in our assessment, the larger cultural cost — and it is the hardest to unwind if we are wrong.

### 5.3 Reinvestment thesis

We recommend committing, publicly, that **55–65% of gross property savings are reinvested** rather than banked: fit-out quality in retained sites, the hub network, gathering travel budgets held at team level, deskless amenity and scheduling technology, tooling, and manager enablement. A programme that visibly returns value to colleagues will be met very differently from one that appears to be a cost exercise wearing the language of flexibility.

### 5.4 Costs that are routinely underestimated

- **Gathering travel.** Organisations typically under-forecast this by 2–3×. Budget €900–1,400 per person per gathering, all-in, and hold the budget at value-stream level with a carbon allocation attached.
- **Allowances and equipment.** Statutory in several jurisdictions (e.g. remote-work allowance obligations, home-workspace duties). Model at €300–650 per desk-based head per year, calibrated locally.
- **Tooling duplication** during transition; **hub and co-working access fees**; **occupancy analytics**; **dilapidations and exit costs** on vacated leases.

---

## 6. Working Agreements: Defaults, Not Blank Pages

Handing thousands of teams a blank page produces uneven quality and consumes manager time we have not budgeted. We therefore recommend **opinionated defaults** that a team can adopt in ten minutes, and deviate from with a one-paragraph written rationale.

### 6.1 Published defaults

| Element | Default | Deviation |
|---|---|---|
| Core overlap | 3 hours per working day across the value stream, rotated (§8.5) | Written rationale; must not push the burden onto one region |
| Meeting-free block | One half-day per week, common across the value stream | Value-stream leader approval |
| In-person cadence | Distributed teams: 4 days per quarter, purpose-stated. Co-located teams: 2 days per week anchor. Hybrid mixed: 1 anchor day per week plus quarterly gathering | Team may increase freely; reduction needs rationale |
| Channel semantics | Chat = today; email = 2 working days; ticket = per SLA; call = decisions, disagreement, relationships | Local adaptation encouraged |
| Meeting hygiene | No status meetings; written pre-read; decisions logged | None |
| Inclusion rule | If one participant is remote, all join individually | None — this is a global non-negotiable |
| Review | Quarterly, 45 minutes | None |

### 6.2 Interface protocol (the incompatibility problem)

1. Agreements are authored at the **value stream**, not the team. Teams may add, not contradict.
2. Where two interdependent groups conflict, the **more distributed party's constraints take precedence**, because their options are fewer.
3. Conflict is raised in writing to the shared leader; resolution within **5 working days**; outcome recorded in the Register.
4. Unresolved conflicts escalate automatically. No one has to force a confrontation to get a decision — the clock does it, which preserves working relationships between the parties.
5. Each value stream nominates a **working-agreement steward** (not necessarily the manager) who holds the document and convenes the review.

### 6.3 What the agreement covers

Overlap and protected focus time; default channel per work type; what earns synchronous time; response norms and the meaning of silence; the specific purposes of coming together (kickoffs, conflict resolution, design bursts, onboarding, celebration) and the cadence those imply; decision rights; the inclusion check. One to two pages, visible company-wide. The value lies as much in the conversation as in the document.

---

# The Future of Work: A Framework of Principles, Not a Policy

*A working draft — offered as a set of design choices rather than a set of rules. Where it reads as tentative, that's deliberate.*

---

## 0. A reframing worth considering first

Most "future of work" programmes fail in a predictable way: they answer the question *"how many days should people be in the office?"* That question is a proxy, and not a very good one. It measures attendance rather than outcomes, and it invites a global company to impose a single number on wildly different realities — a Tokyo commute, a São Paulo apartment shared with three generations, a Stockholm summer, a Bangalore team that works across four time zones before lunch.

The more productive question is: **what work do we do, what conditions does that work actually require, and who is best placed to judge?**

If the framework below has a spine, it is this: *decisions should be made as close as possible to the people who hold the relevant context, with the centre defining only what genuinely must be common.*

---

## 1. Six Design Principles

**Principle 1 — Purpose over presence.**
Time and location are inputs. Contribution is the output. Wherever the two can be decoupled, decouple them. Where they genuinely cannot (lab work, manufacturing, client sites, regulated environments), say so plainly and explain why — an unexplained constraint tends to be read as an arbitrary one.

**Principle 2 — A thin centre, thick edges.**
The global organisation should own very little: legal and tax compliance, information security, data on equity of outcomes, a shared tooling backbone, and a small number of non-negotiables. Almost everything else — rhythms, meeting norms, office use, collaboration rituals — belongs to teams and regions. A short list of global rules is easier to respect than a long one.

**Principle 3 — The team is the unit of design.**
Individuals working alone rarely produce the friction; mismatched *interfaces between people* do. So the smallest meaningful design unit is the team, and each team should be asked to author its own explicit working agreement (see §3). Teams that write their own rules tend to keep them.

**Principle 4 — Flexibility must be equitably distributed.**
Flexibility that flows to the confident, the senior, the geographically central, or the well-housed is not a benefit — it is a new form of privilege. Assume proximity bias exists until measurement proves otherwise, rather than the reverse.

**Principle 5 — Local adaptation is a feature, not a compliance failure.**
Divergence between Singapore, Munich, and Mexico City is evidence the framework is working. What must be consistent is the *quality of the experience and the fairness of the outcome*, not the shape of the arrangement.

**Principle 6 — Everything is a hypothesis with an expiry date.**
Publish arrangements with review dates attached. A policy that is explicitly provisional invites honest feedback; a policy presented as permanent invites quiet workarounds. Reversibility is cheaper than certainty.

---

## 2. The Architecture: Four Concentric Layers

| Layer | Owns | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Global core** (deliberately minimal) | Non-negotiables | Employment/tax compliance, security standards, pay and promotion equity, tooling backbone, data & measurement, ethical floor (right to disconnect, accessibility) |
| **Regional / country layer** | Legal and cultural translation | Statutory consultation (works councils, unions), local labour law, office portfolio decisions, allowances calibrated to local cost and housing reality, public holiday and time-zone conventions |
| **Team layer** | The real design work | Collaboration agreement: core overlap hours, meeting-free blocks, async defaults, in-person cadence and *purpose*, decision-rights map, response-time expectations |
| **Individual layer** | Personal fit | Where and when within the team agreement, workspace setup, focus/collaboration balance, negotiated exceptions (caregiving, health, accessibility, visa constraints) |

The layers cascade in one direction only: an outer layer may *constrain* an inner one, but it should have to justify doing so. That justification requirement is the mechanism that keeps the centre thin.

---

## 3. The Team Working Agreement

A single artefact, one or two pages, authored by the team, visible to anyone in the company. It answers roughly:

- **Overlap:** which hours do we genuinely need to share, and which are we protecting for deep work?
- **Default channel:** what belongs in writing? What belongs in a call? What belongs in a room?
- **Meeting economics:** what earns synchronous time — decisions, disagreement, relationship-building? What doesn't — status updates, information transfer?
- **Response norms:** what is "urgent" here, and what is not? What does silence mean?
- **In-person purpose:** what specific things do we come together *for* — kickoffs, conflict resolution, design bursts, onboarding, celebration — and how often does that imply?
- **Decision rights:** who decides what, alone, and what genuinely needs consensus?
- **Inclusion check:** if one person is remote, are we all remote-by-default in that meeting?

The value lies less in the document than in the conversation that produces it. Reviewed quarterly; retired when it stops being true.

---

## 4. Cultural Calibration — Without Stereotyping

There is a trap here. National culture models are useful for generating hypotheses and dangerous when used to assign behaviour to individuals. A safer path: use them to know *what to ask about*, then let the answers come from the people themselves.

Dimensions genuinely worth probing, region by region:

- **Physical reality.** Housing size, broadband quality, ambient noise, shared living arrangements, commute length and cost, climate. In several markets this alone determines whether "remote" is a benefit or a burden.
- **Meaning of the office.** In some contexts an office is a cost centre; in others it is status, social life, an escape from a cramped flat, or the primary channel through which mentorship and advancement flow. Removing it means different things in each.
- **Visibility and advancement.** Where careers are read through presence and informal access, remote work quietly penalises the remote. Where they are read through delivered outcomes, it does not. Know which you are in — and note that the answer may differ between two offices of the same company.
- **Directness and feedback.** In lower-context, more direct environments, written async norms land easily. In higher-context environments, meaning travels through tone, timing, seating, and what is *not* said — so purely text-based coordination can strip out crucial signal. Such teams may need more synchronous time, richer channels, and more explicit invitation to dissent, not less.
- **Relationship to hierarchy.** Where authority is expected to be visible, "decide for yourself" can be experienced as abandonment rather than empowerment. The remedy is usually clearer decision rights and explicit permission, not more supervision.
- **Legal and statutory frame.** Works councils, co-determination, mandated consultation, statutory right-to-disconnect, remote-work allowance requirements, home-office inspection duties. In some jurisdictions the framework must be *negotiated*, not announced — build that time into the plan.
- **Family and social obligation.** School hours, elder care, multi-generational households, religious observance, seasonal migration patterns.

**Method matters more than the model.** Prefer listening structures over survey instruments alone: small mixed-level listening sessions, local "work design" volunteers drawn by interest rather than title, anonymous channels for the things people won't say to a manager, and close attention to what people *do* — badge data, tool telemetry, attrition and internal-mobility patterns — versus what they say. Divergence between the two is the most interesting data you will get.

---

## 5. Space: The Office as Destination

If people can work anywhere, the office must earn the journey.

- **Design for what homes can't offer:** collaboration surfaces, project rooms, social density, ceremony, spontaneous encounter, hospitality — not rows of individual desks people travel an hour to sit at.
- **Portfolio, not headquarters:** a mix of anchor offices, smaller regional hubs, co-working access, and gathering venues for periodic team assembly. Ask whether one large building or three small ones better serves the same population.
- **Booking that reveals intent:** let people see *who* and *what* rather than just *how many seats*. Presence follows people, not floorplans.
- **Equip for hybrid honestly:** every room a remote participant can join as an equal — good audio first, camera second, a shared digital surface always. A badly equipped room silently teaches people that remote colleagues don't count.
- **Read the utilisation data as a signal, not a verdict:** low attendance may mean the work doesn't need the room, or it may mean the room is bad.

---

## 6. Tools and Information Architecture

Fewer tools, clearer purposes:

- **A single source of truth** for decisions and documents — findable without asking a person.
- **Written-first by default.** Decisions, rationale, and context in durable text; this is also the primary accessibility, inclusion, and time-zone equaliser.
- **Async as the baseline, sync as the deliberate choice.** Recorded and summarised sessions where the topic allows.
- **Explicit channel semantics.** Which tool means "now", which means "today", which means "when you get to it". Ambiguity here is the main cause of always-on anxiety.
- **Multilingual reality.** Translation, transcripts, glossaries, and a norm that fluency in the corporate language is not a proxy for competence.
- **Restraint on monitoring.** Activity surveillance buys a little short-term comfort and spends a great deal of trust. Measure outputs; leave keystrokes alone.

---

## 7. Managing, Careers, and Equity

- Shift management from supervision to **outcome-setting, context-sharing, and unblocking**. Invest in this — it is the single largest capability gap, and the most common point of failure.
- **Onboarding and early careers deserve special treatment.** Tacit learning is the first casualty of distributed work. Deliberate cohorts, structured shadowing, and front-loaded in-person time.
- **Audit for proximity bias annually**: promotion rate, pay progression, high-visibility project allocation, and attrition — segmented by location and by work pattern. Publish the results internally. Sunlight does most of the work.
- **Sponsorship, not just mentorship**, for those furthest from the centre of gravity.

---

## 8. Guardrails Worth Naming Explicitly

Permanent cross-border remote work creates real exposure: permanent-establishment risk, payroll and social-security obligations, immigration status, data residency, insurance, and health-and-safety duties for home workspaces. The pragmatic answer is usually a **tiered mobility policy** — generous short-term "work from anywhere" windows within defined jurisdictions and day limits; case-by-case review beyond that; a small list of countries where the answer is simply no, with the reason stated.

Compensation is the other live wire. Choose a philosophy deliberately — location-based, zone-based, or role-based — and be able to defend it in public, because you will have to.

---

## 9. Sequencing

| Phase | Focus |
|---|---|
| **Discovery (~6–10 weeks)** | Listening sessions and diagnostics across regions; map work types to genuine co-location needs; audit legal constraints; baseline the equity metrics |
| **Design (~6 weeks)** | Publish the thin global core; regions translate; teams draft their first agreements |
| **Pilots (1–2 quarters)** | Deliberately varied experiments — a fully distributed team, an office-anchored one, a "quarterly gathering" model, a four-day variant. Pilots include a *sunset date* and an agreed set of signals |
| **Scale and prune (ongoing)** | Keep what worked, retire what didn't, publish both. Annual review of the core |

Signals worth watching: quality and speed of decisions, cycle time, cross-team collaboration, voluntary attrition by segment, offer acceptance rates, internal mobility, onboarding time-to-contribution, self-reported energy and belonging, and the equity audit. Deliberately *not* watching: hours logged, badge swipes as a performance measure, green status dots.

---

## 10. Questions Left Deliberately Open

These are for the organisation to answer, not the framework:

- If two teams reach opposite conclusions about in-person work, is that a problem to resolve — or evidence the system is functioning?
- What is the smallest set of global rules you could live with? Have you tried removing one?
- Where a local practice conflicts with a global value — around visibility, hierarchy, or feedback — which yields, and who decides?
- What would you need to see to conclude, honestly, that this framework was wrong?
- And perhaps the quietest question: is leadership prepared to be bound by the same arrangements it designs for everyone else?

---

*The most useful thing this document can do is provoke better local answers than the ones it contains. Treat it as a first iteration; the second should not come from the centre.*

Make this a seventh principle, not a footnote.

**2. There is no economics in the document at all.**
No real estate cost base, no lease expiry ladder, no capital commitments, no allowance cost modelling, no target savings or reinvestment logic, no business case. Real estate is typically the second- or third-largest cost line; a re-evaluation of "where people work" that never mentions money will not survive its first executive review.

Quality will vary enormously, manager time cost is significant, and there is no mechanism for the obvious failure mode: **interdependent teams with incompatible agreements** (Team A's meeting-free Friday is Team B's only overlap window).

The document repeatedly reaches the hard question and steps back: compensation philosophy ("choose one, deliberately"), local-vs-global value conflicts, the resolution of divergent team conclusions. The caveat is good; the practice slips. ---

- The reframing away from "how many days" toward work-type requirements — correct and well argued.
- The four-layer architecture with a justification burden on the centre — a good structural idea, needing only operational teeth.
- §4's methodological caution about culture models, and the emphasis on observed behaviour versus stated preference.
- §5's "office must earn the journey" and the point that low utilisation may indict the room, not the model.
- §6's explicit channel semantics as the cure for always-on anxiety — sharp and practical.
- §7's proximity-bias audit and sponsorship-over-mentorship distinction.
- §8's tiered mobility policy — the correct pragmatic answer.
- The anti-metrics list (hours logged, green dots) — worth keeping verbatim.

---

## E. Suggested restructure

1. One-page executive summary with the actual recommendation and the money.
2. Seven principles (add flexibility-for-all across deskless and desk-based).
3. Four-layer architecture **plus** governance, decision rights, exceptions and escalation.
4. Portfolio and financial case, anchored to the lease expiry calendar.
5. Team agreements — with published defaults and an interface protocol.
6. Local calibration: method, legal track, consultation calendar.
7. Space, tools (with residency/privacy constraints), and security.
8. Manager and leader enablement — expanded substantially.
9. Compensation, mobility and tax — with a recommended position.
10. Scorecard, roadmap (Phase 0 = leadership alignment), and named owners.
11. Risks, reversal triggers, and stability commitments to employees.

---

Permanent cross-border remote work creates real exposure: permanent-establishment risk, payroll and social-security obligations, immigration status, data residency, insurance, and health-and-safety duties for home workspaces. The pragmatic answer is usually a **tiered mobility policy** — generous short-term "work from anywhere" windows within defined jurisdictions and day limits; case-by-case review beyond that; a small list of countries where the answer is simply no, with the reason stated.

Compensation is the other live wire. Choose a philosophy deliberately — location-based, zone-based, or role-based — and be able to defend it in public, because you will have to.

---

## 9. Sequencing

| Phase | Focus |
|---|---|
| **Discovery (~6–10 weeks)** | Listening sessions and diagnostics across regions; map work types to genuine co-location needs; audit legal constraints; baseline the equity metrics |
| **Design (~6 weeks)** | Publish the thin global core; regions translate; teams draft their first agreements |
| **Pilots (1–2 quarters)** | Deliberately varied experiments — a fully distributed team, an office-anchored one, a "quarterly gathering" model, a four-day variant. Pilots include a *sunset date* and an agreed set of signals |
| **Scale and prune (ongoing)** | Keep what worked, retire what didn't, publish both. Annual review of the core |

Signals worth watching: quality and speed of decisions, cycle time, cross-team collaboration, voluntary attrition by segment, offer acceptance rates, internal mobility, onboarding time-to-contribution, self-reported energy and belonging, and the equity audit. Deliberately *not* watching: hours logged, badge swipes as a performance measure, green status dots.

---

## 10. Questions Left Deliberately Open

These are for the organisation to answer, not the framework:

- If two teams reach opposite conclusions about in-person work, is that a problem to resolve — or evidence the system is functioning?
- What is the smallest set of global rules you could live with? Have you tried removing one?
- Where a local practice conflicts with a global value — around visibility, hierarchy, or feedback — which yields, and who decides?
- What would you need to see to conclude, honestly, that this framework was wrong?
- And perhaps the quietest question: is leadership prepared to be bound by the same arrangements it designs for everyone else?

---

*The most useful thing this document can do is provoke better local answers than the ones it contains. Treat it as a first iteration; the second should not come from the centre.*

# Critique: "The Future of Work: A Framework of Principles, Not a Policy"

**Summary judgement:** Intellectually strong, well-organised, and unusually good at avoiding the standard traps (attendance-day mandates, crude national-culture stereotyping). But it is a *thought piece* where the request called for a *design*. It under-serves three constituencies that will decide whether this ever ships — the CFO, the deskless workforce, and the manager who has to run it on Monday — and it resolves none of the hard trade-offs it correctly identifies.

---

## A. Critical gaps (must fix)

**1. The deskless / frontline workforce is essentially absent.**
A "large international company" almost certainly has manufacturing, logistics, retail, field service, labs, or contact centres. Principle 1 dismisses them in half a sentence ("say so plainly and explain why"). This is the single biggest flaw. As written, the framework hands autonomy, allowances, and "work from anywhere" windows to knowledge workers and offers frontline staff an explanation. That is a recipe for a two-tier culture and a union grievance.
**Fix:** Add a parallel track — *flexibility for all, in different currencies*. For deskless roles: predictable scheduling with advance notice, self-service shift swapping, compressed schedules, banked time, on-site amenity and quiet-space investment, and a stated commitment that flexibility budget per head is comparable across populations even if its form differs. Make this a seventh principle, not a footnote.

**2. There is no economics in the document at all.**
No real estate cost base, no lease expiry ladder, no capital commitments, no allowance cost modelling, no target savings or reinvestment logic, no business case. Real estate is typically the second- or third-largest cost line; a re-evaluation of "where people work" that never mentions money will not survive its first executive review.
**Fix:** Add a section covering (a) current portfolio cost and lease expiry profile as the *forcing calendar* for decisions, (b) a portfolio scenario model (consolidate / regionalise / hub-and-spoke) with cost, headcount capacity and risk per scenario, (c) reinvestment thesis — savings redirected to fit-out quality, hubs, gathering budgets, tooling, (d) total cost of a flexible model including allowances, travel for in-person gatherings (frequently underestimated by 2–3x), and duplicated tooling.

**3. Zero governance.** Section 10 asks "who decides?" and leaves it open. That is abdication presented as humility. Someone must own this, fund it, arbitrate conflicts, and be accountable for the equity audit.
**Fix:** Propose a concrete default — a Work Design Council (HR, Real Estate, IT, Legal/Tax, Security, plus rotating regional and non-managerial members), a named executive owner, a quarterly cadence, an explicit escalation and exception path with SLAs, and a published decision-rights matrix (RACI) across the four layers. The "outer layer must justify constraining inner" mechanism is rhetorically appealing but operationally undefined: justify to whom, on what standard, with what appeal?

**4. Team agreements are a blank page handed to thousands of teams.**
Section 3 is the best idea in the document and the least implementable. Quality will vary enormously, manager time cost is significant, and there is no mechanism for the obvious failure mode: **interdependent teams with incompatible agreements** (Team A's meeting-free Friday is Team B's only overlap window).
**Fix:** (a) Ship *opinionated defaults* teams can adopt in ten minutes and deviate from with a written rationale — e.g., a default 3-hour overlap band per value stream, a default in-person cadence of N days per quarter, default channel semantics. Defaults beat blank pages. (b) Define an *interface protocol*: agreements are set at the value-stream/interdependency level, not the org-chart team; the more distributed party's constraints take precedence; conflicts escalate to the shared leader within five working days.

**5. Decisiveness deficit.**
The document repeatedly reaches the hard question and steps back: compensation philosophy ("choose one, deliberately"), local-vs-global value conflicts, the resolution of divergent team conclusions. The client asked for a proposal. Meta-commentary such as "where it reads as tentative, that's deliberate" and "the second should not come from the centre" reads as elegant, but a leadership team cannot act on it.
**Fix:** Take positions with stated rationale and reversibility. On pay, for example: role-based within geographic zones; no reduction for existing employees who stay within zone; adjustment only on zone change with 12-month grandfathering; explicit anti-arbitrage rule. State it, defend it, and note the conditions under which you'd revisit.

---

## B. Significant weaknesses

**6. Internal contradiction on timeline.** Section 4 correctly warns that in some jurisdictions the framework must be *negotiated*, not announced. Section 9 then allocates six weeks to design. German, Dutch, French, Austrian and Nordic works council consultation on working-time and monitoring matters routinely runs 3–9 months. Either the timeline is wrong or the framework will be imposed illegally in Europe.
**Fix:** Split the sequence into a global track and a parallel co-determination track with its own realistic calendar; make explicit which elements can be launched pending consultation and which cannot. Also note that lease decisions run on a multi-year clock that will not wait for pilots — some property calls must be made on scenario logic before the pilots report.

**7. Metrics are listed, not operationalised.** No baselines, targets, data sources, owners, or cadence. "Quality and speed of decisions" is unmeasurable as stated. Publishing equity-audit results internally has legal and works-council implications in several jurisdictions that are not examined.
**Fix:** Convert to a one-page scorecard: metric, definition, source system, baseline, target, owner, review cadence. Propose proxies for the soft ones (e.g., decision latency from a decision log; rework rate; cross-team dependency cycle time).

**8. Privacy and data-residency conflicts unflagged.**
- §5's "booking that reveals *who*" is colleague-location visibility. Works councils in Germany and elsewhere have blocked precisely this; it also has GDPR implications. Needs opt-in design and consultation.
- §6's "single source of truth" collides with data residency and localisation requirements (China, Russia, EU sovereignty demands, regulated sectors). A single global platform may be legally impossible; the framework should say how it handles a federated reality.
- §4 endorses "badge data and tool telemetry" analysis two sections before §6 warns against monitoring. Reconcile: aggregate, anonymised, threshold-limited, consulted-upon, never individual-level.

**9. Perpetual provisionality has a human cost.** Principle 6 ("everything is a hypothesis with an expiry date") is right for the organisation and destabilising for employees, who make housing, schooling and eldercare decisions on the back of these arrangements. Reversibility without stability guarantees produces exactly the quiet workarounds the principle claims to prevent.
**Fix:** Pair it with a stability commitment — e.g., a minimum 6–12 months' notice for any material reduction in an individual's location flexibility, and no retroactive changes.

**10. Only a defensive business case.** The framing is fairness, accommodation and risk. Missing entirely: the *offensive* value — expanded hiring radius into new talent markets, labour-cost arbitrage, employer brand and offer-acceptance advantage, follow-the-sun capability, resilience/BCP, carbon footprint reduction against stated ESG targets. This is what converts the programme from an HR cost item into a strategy item.

**11. Manager enablement is named as the largest capability gap and given four lines.** No curriculum, no delivery model, no time budget, no assessment, no link to promotion criteria. If this is truly the top failure point, it deserves the most detailed section, not one of the shortest.

**12. Leadership alignment appears only as a rhetorical closing question.** Executive misalignment (or a CEO reversal eighteen months in) is the most common cause of death for these programmes. It belongs as **Phase 0** — a documented leadership commitment on their own working pattern, on the review triggers, and on what would and would not cause a reversal.

**13. Self-contradiction in §4.** The section warns against national-culture models, then deploys high-context/low-context and power-distance framings — which are national-culture models. The caveat is good; the practice slips. Either own the models as explicit hypothesis-generators with named sources and known limitations, or replace them with observable, testable variables (housing, broadband, commute, promotion patterns by location).

**14. Time-zone burden is not treated as an equity issue.** The document handles proximity bias well but ignores the systematic cost borne by whichever region always takes the 22:00 call. This is a concrete, measurable, fixable unfairness.
**Fix:** Mandate rotation of meeting times across time zones, cap out-of-hours synchronous obligations per person per month, and measure it.

# The Future of Work: A Design Proposal for Global Endorsement and Local Adaptation

**Prepared for:** Executive Committee, with parallel circulation to Regional Leadership, Group Finance, Real Estate, IT, Legal & Tax, Group Security, and — where statutory bodies exist — to works councils and employee representatives *before* any external communication.

**Status:** Recommended design. All financial figures are illustrative placeholders pending validation by Group Finance and Real Estate; all statutory timelines require confirmation by local Legal counsel. Sections marked **[Requires consultation]** are not to be presented as decided in the affected jurisdictions.

---

## 1. Executive Summary

**The recommendation in three lines.** Stop asking how many days people should be in the office. Instead, (a) match work type to genuine co-location need, (b) push design decisions to the value-stream level within a deliberately thin global core, and (c) extend a comparable *flexibility investment per head* to desk-based and deskless populations alike — in different currencies, but at similar value.

**What it costs and what it returns (illustrative, to be validated).** For a company of ~60,000 people across ~40 countries, of whom roughly 40% are desk-based:

| Item | 3-year illustrative figure |
|---|---|
| Current annual property cost (rent, service charge, energy, FM) | €430m |
| Leases expiring or with break options within 36 months | ~34% of portfolio by cost |
| Net property saving from recommended portfolio scenario (regional hub-and-spoke) | €95–130m p.a. by year 3 |
| Reinvestment: fit-out quality, hub network, gathering travel, tooling, deskless amenity and scheduling systems | €55–70m p.a. |
| Home-working allowances and equipment (desk-based) | €18–24m p.a. |
| Manager and leader enablement (build + delivery) | €9m one-off, €3m p.a. |
| **Net structural saving retained** | **€25–45m p.a.** |

**Where the upside actually sits** — and this is the part that turns the programme from a cost exercise into a strategy one:

- **Hiring radius.** Access to 6–8 additional metropolitan labour markets per region without new legal entities, using the tiered mobility model in §10.
- **Offer acceptance and retention.** Flexibility is now a top-three factor in candidate decisions in most of our markets; a defensible, differentiated position is worth more than the property saving.
- **Follow-the-sun and resilience.** Distributed capability materially improves business continuity and reduces single-site concentration risk.
- **Carbon.** Commuting and portfolio reduction contribute measurably to stated Scope 1–3 targets; the offsetting increase in gathering travel must be counted honestly (see §5.4).

**What we ask of the Executive Committee.** Not approval of a rulebook — endorsement of seven principles, a governance body, a property scenario aligned to the lease calendar, and a set of stated positions on pay, mobility and stability. And, in Phase 0, a documented commitment from each Executive Committee member regarding their own working pattern. Nothing else in this document will survive if that step is skipped.

**A note on how we propose to proceed.** This design has been shaped by early listening across regions and, deliberately, has not been finalised. Several elements require formal consultation before they can be presented as decided. We would rather move a quarter more slowly and arrive with agreement intact than announce a scheme that quietly loses the confidence of colleagues and their representatives.

---

## 2. Seven Principles

**Principle 1 — Purpose over presence.**
Time and location are inputs; contribution is the output. Where they can be decoupled, decouple them. Where they genuinely cannot — production lines, laboratories, client sites, regulated environments, secure facilities — the constraint is stated with its reason, and Principle 7 applies instead.

**Principle 2 — A thin centre, thick edges.**
The centre owns only what must be common: legal and tax compliance, security, equity measurement, the tooling backbone, and a short list of non-negotiables. Rhythms, meeting norms, office use and rituals belong closer to the work. A short list of global rules is easier to respect than a long one.

**Principle 3 — The value stream is the unit of design.**
Friction lives in the interfaces between people, not in individuals working alone. Working agreements are therefore authored at the level of interdependency — the value stream, product line or service chain — not the org chart box (§6).

**Principle 4 — Flexibility must be equitably distributed, and measured.**
Flexibility that flows to the senior, the confident, the geographically central or the well-housed is a privilege, not a benefit. We assume proximity bias and time-zone burden exist until measurement shows otherwise.

**Principle 5 — Local adaptation is a feature, not a compliance failure.**
Divergence between Singapore, Munich and Monterrey is evidence the framework is working. What must be consistent is the fairness of outcomes, not the shape of arrangements.

**Principle 6 — Learn openly, but do not destabilise lives.**
Arrangements carry review dates; individuals carry stability guarantees (§12.3). Reversibility at the system level is paired with notice periods at the personal level, because colleagues make housing, schooling and eldercare decisions on the strength of what we tell them.

**Principle 7 — Flexibility for all, in different currencies.**
Every colleague receives a flexibility investment; its form differs by role. For deskless colleagues that means predictability, control over time, and quality of the on-site day. The commitment is that **flexibility investment per head is broadly comparable across populations**, and reported as such. This principle exists to prevent the outcome we consider the single largest risk in the programme: a two-tier culture in which one population receives autonomy and the other receives an explanation.

---

## 3. Two Populations, One Commitment

Roughly 60% of our colleagues cannot choose their location. A framework that speaks only to the other 40% would damage cohesion in exactly the places where cohesion is hardest won — plants, depots, contact centres, retail and field service.

**The deskless flexibility package (recommended standard):**

| Element | Commitment |
|---|---|
| Schedule notice | Rosters published ≥ 3 weeks ahead; no unilateral change inside 7 days without premium |
| Shift swapping | Self-service, peer-to-peer, manager-approved by exception only |
| Compressed and split patterns | Available where safety and coverage permit; requests answered within 10 working days with a reason |
| Banked time / time-account | Accrual and withdrawal within statutory limits, portable across the year |
| Part-remote elements of deskless roles | Training, admin, planning, debriefs shifted off-site where feasible — typically 5–15% of hours |
| On-site quality | Quiet rooms, decent break space, lockers, connectivity, parking/transport support, heating and cooling |
| Voice | Frontline representation on the Work Design Council; site-level design volunteers |
| Career access | Remote-accessible training and internal mobility; no advancement path that requires relocation without support |

**Reporting.** The equity scorecard (§11) reports flexibility investment per head, request-approval rates, and schedule-stability performance separately for deskless and desk-based populations. Where a gap opens, it is a Council agenda item, not a footnote.

**[Requires consultation]** In unionised sites, scheduling and time-account provisions are subject to collective bargaining. We recommend approaching representatives with the *principle* and a genuine blank on the mechanism, rather than a finished scheme.

---

## 4. Architecture and Governance

### 4.1 The four layers

| Layer | Owns | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Global core** (minimal) | Non-negotiables | Employment/tax compliance, security standards, pay and promotion equity, tooling backbone, measurement, ethical floor (accessibility, rest and disconnection with the on-call carve-out in §8.4) |
| **Region / country** | Legal and cultural translation | Statutory consultation, labour law, office portfolio, allowances calibrated to local cost and housing, holiday and time-zone conventions |
| **Value stream / team** | The real design work | Working agreement: overlap band, meeting-free blocks, async defaults, in-person cadence and purpose, decision rights, response norms |
| **Individual** | Personal fit | Where and when within the agreement, workspace, negotiated exceptions (caregiving, health, accessibility, visa) |

An outer layer may constrain an inner one, but must record why. Operationally: the constraint is logged in the Work Design Register with a named owner, a category (legal / security / customer coverage / cost / safety), and a review date. Unrecorded constraints lapse at the next quarterly review. Appeals go to the Council, which answers within 15 working days.

### 4.2 Governance

**Work Design Council.** Chaired by the Chief People Officer; sponsored by the COO as named Executive owner. Members: HR, Real Estate & Workplace, IT, Legal & Tax, Group Security, Finance, plus **six rotating seats** — three regional representatives and three non-managerial colleagues (at least one deskless). Quarterly, with a monthly working group.

**Decision rights (summary RACI):**

| Decision | Accountable | Consulted |
|---|---|---|
| Global non-negotiables; ethical floor | Executive Committee | Council; employee representatives |
| Portfolio scenario, capital, lease action | Real Estate, with CFO | Region; Council |
| Country policy translation; allowances | Regional HR lead | Legal; works council; Finance |
| Working agreements; in-person cadence | Value-stream leader | Interdependent teams; team members |
| Individual arrangements | Line manager | HR partner where an exception applies |
| Cross-border remote requests | Global Mobility | Tax, Legal, Security |
| Exceptions and appeals | Work Design Council | Requesting party |

**Service levels.** Individual arrangement requests: answered in 10 working days. Cross-border requests: 20. Escalated inter-team conflicts: resolved by the shared leader within 5 working days, or referred upward automatically. Silence is not an answer; unanswered requests default to "granted provisionally, pending review."

## 5. Property Portfolio and the Financial Case

### 5.1 The lease calendar is the forcing function

Property decisions run on a multi-year clock that will not wait for pilot results. We therefore recommend sequencing decisions by expiry, not by programme phase:

| Horizon | Portfolio share (illustrative) | Recommended posture |
|---|---|---|
| 0–12 months | 11% by cost | Decide now on scenario logic; prefer short extensions to preserve optionality |
| 12–36 months | 23% | Decide by end of Design phase; pilots inform fit-out, not footprint |
| 36 months+ | 66% | Decide after pilots; use the interval to improve occupancy data |

### 5.2 Scenarios

| Scenario | Footprint change | Annual cost effect | Capacity | Principal risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Hold** | 0% | – | 100% | Pays for empty space; signals no change |
| **B. Consolidate to fewer, larger sites** | –25% | –€105m | 70% at 1:1.4 sharing | Longer commutes; concentration risk; poorest fit with local housing realities |
| **C. Regional hub-and-spoke** *(recommended)* | –22% desk area, +14 small hubs | –€95m gross, –€60m net of hub cost and fit-out | 85% at 1:1.6 | Operational complexity; requires disciplined booking data |
| **D. Radical distributed** | –45% | –€180m | 45% | High attrition risk in offices that function as social and mentorship centres; hard to reverse |

We recommend **C**, on grounds of reversibility and reduced disruption to established site communities. D produces the larger number and, in our assessment, the larger cultural cost — and it is the hardest to unwind if we are wrong.

### 5.3 Reinvestment thesis

We recommend committing, publicly, that **55–65% of gross property savings are reinvested** rather than banked: fit-out quality in retained sites, the hub network, gathering travel budgets held at team level, deskless amenity and scheduling technology, tooling, and manager enablement. A programme that visibly returns value to colleagues will be met very differently from one that appears to be a cost exercise wearing the language of flexibility.

### 5.4 Costs that are routinely underestimated

- **Gathering travel.** Organisations typically under-forecast this by 2–3×. Budget €900–1,400 per person per gathering, all-in, and hold the budget at value-stream level with a carbon allocation attached.
- **Allowances and equipment.** Statutory in several jurisdictions (e.g. remote-work allowance obligations, home-workspace duties). Model at €300–650 per desk-based head per year, calibrated locally.
- **Tooling duplication** during transition; **hub and co-working access fees**; **occupancy analytics**; **dilapidations and exit costs** on vacated leases.

## 6. Working Agreements: Defaults, Not Blank Pages

Handing thousands of teams a blank page produces uneven quality and consumes manager time we have not budgeted. We therefore recommend **opinionated defaults** that a team can adopt in ten minutes, and deviate from with a one-paragraph written rationale.

### 6.1 Published defaults

| Element | Default | Deviation |
|---|---|---|
| Core overlap | 3 hours per working day across the value stream, rotated (§8.5) | Written rationale; must not push the burden onto one region |
| Meeting-free block | One half-day per week, common across the value stream | Value-stream leader approval |
| In-person cadence | Distributed teams: 4 days per quarter, purpose-stated. Co-located teams: 2 days per week anchor. Hybrid mixed: 1 anchor day per week plus quarterly gathering | Team may increase freely; reduction needs rationale |
| Channel semantics | Chat = today; email = 2 working days; ticket = per SLA; call = decisions, disagreement, relationships | Local adaptation encouraged |
| Meeting hygiene | No status meetings; written pre-read; decisions logged | None |
| Inclusion rule | If one participant is remote, all join individually | None — this is a global non-negotiable |
| Review | Quarterly, 45 minutes | None |

### 6.2 Interface protocol (the incompatibility problem)

1. Agreements are authored at the **value stream**, not the team. Teams may add, not contradict.
2. Where two interdependent groups conflict, the **more distributed party's constraints take precedence**, because their options are fewer.
3. Conflict is raised in writing to the shared leader; resolution within **5 working days**; outcome recorded in the Register.
4. Unresolved conflicts escalate automatically. No one has to force a confrontation to get a decision — the clock does it, which preserves working relationships between the parties.
5. Each value stream nominates a **working-agreement steward** (not necessarily the manager) who holds the document and convenes the review.

### 6.3 What the agreement covers

Overlap and protected focus time; default channel per work type; what earns synchronous time; response norms and the meaning of silence; the specific purposes of coming together (kickoffs, conflict resolution, design bursts, onboarding, celebration) and the cadence those imply; decision rights; the inclusion check. One to two pages, visible company-wide. The value lies as much in the conversation as in the document.

---

## 7. Local Calibration: Method, Not Model

### 7.1 Use observable variables first

We propose diagnosing regions primarily through variables we can observe and test, rather than through national-culture typologies:

- **Housing and connectivity:** floor area per person, private workspace availability, shared and multi-generational living, broadband quality, power reliability.
- **Commute:** door-to-door time, cost as a share of pay, safety, seasonal and climate factors.
- **What the office does here:** measured through use — is it desk work, mentorship, social life, refuge from a cramped flat, or status?
- **Promotion and pay patterns by location and work pattern:** the empirical test of whether presence is being rewarded.
- **Attrition, internal mobility, offer acceptance** by site.
- **Care and observance patterns:** school hours, eldercare, religious observance, seasonal migration.
- **Statutory frame:** co-determination rights, working-time law, monitoring restrictions, allowance obligations, home-workspace duties.

### 7.2 Where cultural models are used, use them honestly

Frameworks such as Hofstede, Meyer and GLOBE are **hypothesis generators with known limitations** — they describe country averages, not colleagues, and they age. We recommend citing them explicitly when used, never inferring an individual's preferences from them, and always testing the hypothesis locally. A concrete example: rather than asserting that a given office is "high-context," we ask whether written async decisions there produce more clarification requests and rework than elsewhere — an observable, testable question.

Two hypotheses we do consider worth testing everywhere:
- Where advancement travels through informal access, remote work quietly penalises the remote — and this may differ between two of our own offices in the same country.
- Where authority is expected to be visible, "decide for yourself" can be experienced as abandonment. The remedy is clearer decision rights and explicit permission, not closer supervision.

### 7.3 Listening structures

Small mixed-level sessions; local work-design volunteers drawn by interest rather than title; anonymous channels for what people will not say to a manager; and close attention to what people *do* versus what they say. Divergence between the two is the most useful signal we will get.

**On behavioural data — the boundary.** Occupancy, badge and tool telemetry are used **only** in aggregate, anonymised, with a minimum group size of 20, never at individual level, never for performance assessment, with retention limits published, and — where required — only after formal consultation and agreement. This boundary is a global non-negotiable, so that the analysis in §7.1 and the anti-monitoring stance in §9.4 are not in tension.

### 7.4 The co-determination track

**[Requires consultation]** Working time, location, monitoring and workplace change trigger information, consultation or co-determination rights in Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, France, Belgium, the Nordics and elsewhere. Consultation on these matters routinely runs **3–9 months**, and cannot be compressed by programme enthusiasm.

We therefore recommend two parallel tracks:

| Can proceed globally now | Requires local agreement first |
|---|---|
| Principles and governance | Any monitoring or telemetry use |
| Tooling backbone and security standards | Colleague-visible presence or booking data |
| Voluntary pilots with volunteer teams | Changes to working-time patterns or rosters |
| Manager enablement | Allowance schemes and cost-sharing |
| Equity measurement design | Individual-level policy changes; site closures |

Regions where consultation is required will land 1–3 quarters after others. We recommend accepting that asymmetry openly rather than forcing a common launch date — a synchronised announcement bought at the price of a damaged relationship with employee representatives is a poor trade.

---

## 8. Space, Time and Fairness

### 8.1 The office must earn the journey
Design for what homes cannot offer: collaboration surfaces, project rooms, social density, ceremony, hospitality — not rows of desks people travel an hour to sit at.

### 8.2 Portfolio, not headquarters
Anchor offices, regional hubs, co-working access, and gathering venues for periodic assembly. Ask whether one large building or three smaller ones better serves the same population.

### 8.3 Booking **[Requires consultation]**
Team- and purpose-level visibility ("this value stream is in on Wednesday") is the default. **Individual-level colleague visibility is opt-in only**, off by default, and in co-determination jurisdictions must be agreed before enablement. Presence follows people, but not at the price of ambient location tracking.

Every room must let a remote participant join as an equal: audio first, camera second, shared digital surface always. A poorly equipped room silently teaches colleagues that remote participants do not count. Read low utilisation as a signal, not a verdict — it may mean the work does not need the room, or that the room is bad.

### 8.4 Rest, and the on-call carve-out
Global floor: no expectation of response outside a colleague's stated working hours, and no penalty for non-response. **Carve-out:** genuine on-call and follow-the-sun rotations, which must be (a) rostered and published, (b) compensated per local practice, (c) rotated equitably, (d) capped per person per month, and (e) agreed with representatives where required.

### 8.5 Time-zone burden as an equity issue
The colleague who always takes the 22:00 call is paying a real, measurable cost that our proximity-bias audit alone would miss.

- Recurring cross-region meetings **rotate** their time on a published schedule.
- Cap: **no more than 4 out-of-hours synchronous obligations per person per month** without compensating time.
- The scorecard reports out-of-hours meeting load by region and by seniority. If the load sits permanently in one geography, the design is wrong, not the people.
